screens.title: Layered Security: Building the perimeter and interior
screens.narratorSegment: A layered security approach combines complementary controls to reduce risk, avoid single points of failure, and make incident response more effective. Start with security groups and network ACLs at the instance and subnet levels to provide basic filtering by port and IP. Add a perimeter layer that inspects HTTP traffic using an application firewall to stop exploits targeted at your code. Behind that, place a managed network firewall to perform deeper packet inspection and apply organization-wide policies. Finally, enable telemetry—VPC Flow Logs—to verify that policies are working and to investigate anomalies. A concrete example: an internet-facing web app can be fronted by an ALB with an attached WAF Web ACL blocking S Q L injection attempts. Shield Standard automatically mitigates most large floods at the network layer, and if the app is business-critical you would subscribe to Shield Advanced for DDoS response and cost protection. A common misconception is that more rules always improve security; in practice, overly aggressive rules can block legitimate traffic such as DNS and health checks. Testing changes in a staging environment and using count mode before blocking helps avoid outages. The key takeaway: design boundaries where they are most effective, collect telemetry to validate behavior, and plan rollback steps for any enforcement change.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Layered Security
Process Flow

Design steps

  1. Instance layer: Security Groups and NACLs for port and IP controls.
  2. Application layer: WAF to inspect HTTP content and block SQLi/XSS.
  3. Network boundary: Network Firewall for stateless/stateful rules and IPS-like checks.
  4. DDoS mitigation: Shield for volumetric and protocol attacks.
  5. Telemetry: VPC Flow Logs for auditing and investigations.
Key Takeaway

Layering reduces single points of failure and gives you the telemetry you need to validate protections.

Example
Scenario: public web application behind an ALB. The ALB receives HTTP requests, WAF inspects and blocks SQL injection patterns, Shield reduces the impact of SYN and UDP floods, and Network Firewall enforces company-wide egress policies for inter-VPC traffic.
Why WAF
Stops application exploits that target input parsing and session handling.
Why Network Firewall
Provides deep inspection and centralized policy enforcement across VPCs.
Common mistake
Blocking without testing: aggressive rules can block DNS or health checks. Use count or monitoring modes before blocking in production.

screens.title: AWS WAF fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: AWS WAF is an application-layer filter that inspects HTTP and HTTPS requests to web applications and APIs. It looks at IP addresses, HTTP headers, the request body, and URI strings to match patterns associated with attacks such as S Q L injection or cross-site scripting. You can write custom rules for precise control, or attach managed rule groups curated by AWS or third parties for common protections. Managed rule groups are useful when you want fast coverage for known vulnerability classes without authoring detailed patterns yourself. When a request matches a rule, WAF can take one of three actions: allow, block, or count for monitoring. A practical example: attach a managed SQLi rule group to a Web ACL protecting an ALB that fronts an A P I. The WAF will examine incoming requests and block those matching the S Q L injection patterns, returning a 403 response. A misunderstanding to avoid is thinking WAF replaces code-level validation; WAF reduces attack surface but input validation and secure coding remain necessary. Always enable visibility configuration to send sampled requests and metrics to CloudWatch so you can tune rules based on real traffic.

keyIdea.title: Application-layer filtering
keyIdea.text: WAF inspects HTTP/S requests and uses custom or managed rules to allow, block, or count matching requests.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › AWS WAF fundamentals
Definition

What WAF does

WAF inspects HTTP/S requests and applies rules that match IPs, headers, body contents, or URI strings to detect common web exploits.

Actions
Allow, Block, or Count. Use count to tune rules before blocking in production.
Managed Rule Groups
Curated protections for common classes like SQL injection or XSS so you don't need to write every rule.
Concrete Example
Attach the "AWS Managed Rules for SQL database" rule group to a Web ACL for an ALB. When a malicious request contains SQL injection patterns the rule matches and the action blocks the request, typically returning a 403 Forbidden response.
Misconception
WAF is not a substitute for secure coding and validation; it reduces exposure but does not fix application bugs.
Key Takeaway

Use WAF for Layer 7 protections, prefer managed rule groups when you need fast coverage, and monitor before blocking.

screens.title: WAF rule types and tuning
screens.narratorSegment: WAF offers a flexible rule model. You can create rules that match on IP addresses, HTTP headers, URI strings, and request bodies. Rules may look for signature patterns that indicate S Q L injection or cross-site scripting. Managed rule groups give you an easy starting point — for example, a S Q L database managed rule group targets S Q L injection patterns so you do not have to author every detection pattern yourself. Start with managed protections in count mode to see what traffic would have been blocked and tune the rule priorities before switching to block. Use IP sets to block or allow ranges quickly. For custom rules, think about rule order and priorities because WAF evaluates rules based on priority. A concrete tuning example: deploy the managed SQLi rule group and monitor CloudWatch metrics for the Web ACL; if you see many false positives from a legitimate bot, add a conditional rule to allow that bot's user agent or IP range. A frequent error is setting a broad block action that inadvertently denies legitimate health checks or partners. Always validate rules with sampled request logs and plan a rollback path in case a change disrupts availability.

keyIdea.text: Use managed rules in count mode, monitor metrics, and add allow exceptions to reduce false positives before blocking traffic.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › WAF Rule Tuning
Rule Types
  • IP match conditions and IP sets for known bad or trusted addresses.
  • Header and user-agent conditions to allow or block based on client identity.
  • URI and body inspection for SQL injection, XSS, and other payload patterns.
  • Managed rule groups for fast coverage of common threats.
Tuning workflow
  1. Enable managed rule in count mode.
  2. Review sampled requests and CloudWatch metrics.
  3. Add allow conditions for false positives or adjust rule priority.
  4. Switch to block when confident.
Scenario
A managed SQLi rule flags many requests from a crawler. You examine sampled requests, note the crawler's user-agent and IP range, and then create an allow rule for that IP set before switching the SQLi rule to block mode.
Common mistake
Changing rule action to block immediately without monitoring causes service interruptions for legitimate clients.
Key Takeaway

Observe impacts in count mode and tune exceptions before enforcing blocks.

screens.title: AWS Shield: Standard vs Advanced
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Shield provides DDoS protection at different levels. Shield Standard is automatic and free for all customers. It provides always-on detection and inline mitigation for common Layer 3 and Layer 4 attacks, such as SYN floods, UDP floods, and amplification attacks, and it works transparently with CloudFront, Route 53, and load balancers. Shield Advanced is a paid tier intended for business-critical applications. It offers near real-time attack visibility, engages the AWS DDoS Response Team for proactive mitigation, and includes cost protection to cover scaling charges that occur during an attack. Shield Advanced also integrates with WAF so that the response team can suggest or deploy custom WAF rules during an attack. A common confusion is to assume Shield Advanced prevents every possible outage; it significantly improves detection and response but must be combined with WAF and network controls as part of a layered design. For most standard workloads, Shield Standard is sufficient; for high-value services with strict availability requirements, Shield Advanced provides operational support and financial protections that justify its use. AWS Shield: Standard vs Advanced means shield standard is automatic; shield advanced adds visibility, drt support, and cost protections for critical workloads.. In practical terms, choose the right ddos protection tier. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › AWS Shield Comparison
Shield Standard
Always-on detection and inline mitigation for common network and transport layer attacks. No additional configuration or cost is required and it integrates with CloudFront, Route 53, and load balancers.
Use when
You need baseline protection for standard workloads and public endpoints.
Shield Advanced
Provides enhanced detection, near real-time visibility, access to the AWS DDoS Response Team, and financial protections for scaling costs. It integrates with WAF for coordinated mitigation during major attacks.
Use when
You operate business-critical services where availability and rapid response are top priorities.
Decision guide
Cost
Standard: none. Advanced: paid service with additional protections.
Response
Advanced includes DRT engagement and custom mitigation support.
Visibility
Advanced gives near real-time attack metrics and integration with WAF for targeted rules.

screens.title: AWS Network Firewall overview
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Network Firewall is a managed network and transport layer service that filters traffic moving through VPC boundaries. It supports both stateless rules, which examine packets independently for fast filtering, and stateful rules, which track connections and enable deeper inspection of protocols and application behavior. Stateful rules are useful when you need to make decisions based on connection state or application-layer knowledge, such as allowing established TLS flows or inspecting HTTP headers. Network Firewall can be deployed in a centralized security VPC so that traffic from many VPCs is routed through a single enforcement point via Transit Gateway. This centralization simplifies policy consistency and compliance. A practical scenario: route all egress traffic from development VPCs through the security VPC where Network Firewall enforces outbound domain and port rules, preventing data exfiltration to risky hosts. A common misunderstanding is treating Network Firewall as a replacement for WAF; instead, they complement each other: WAF handles Layer 7 web application threats, while Network Firewall enforces network-level policies and can perform intrusion prevention tasks. AWS Network Firewall overview means network firewall provides stateless and stateful filtering and fits well in a centralized security vpc for consistent policy enforcement.. In practical terms, centralized vpc boundary enforcement. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Network Firewall
Definition

What it enforces

Network Firewall filters at the network and transport layers with stateless packet filters and stateful rules that track connections for deeper protocol-aware inspection.
Stateless rules
Fast packet filters that do not track connection state; useful for IP and port blocks.
Stateful rules
Track sessions and inspect protocols like HTTP or TLS for more precise control.
Concrete Use
Centralize inspection by routing traffic through a security VPC. Use stateless rules at high volumes for quick filtering and stateful rules where connection context matters.
Misconception
Network Firewall does not replace WAF; it complements WAF by handling network-level threats and IPS-like functions.
Key Takeaway

Use Network Firewall for centralized, scalable network filtering and pair it with WAF for application-layer protection.

screens.title: Centralized inspection with a security VPC
screens.narratorSegment: Centralized inspection uses a security VPC that hosts Network Firewall and other monitoring appliances. Traffic from application or data VPCs is routed through a Transit Gateway to the security VPC, creating a single enforcement point for ingress, egress, and inter-VPC flows. This architecture simplifies policy management because you maintain rules in one place instead of spread across multiple VPCs. A concrete scenario: route egress traffic from several development VPCs to the security VPC where Network Firewall enforces outbound deny lists and inspects HTTPS connections for suspicious domains. Ensure routing and NAT are configured so that return traffic flows back through the inspection path. A common pitfall is creating asymmetric routing where return packets bypass the firewall, which prevents stateful rules from working correctly. Test the routing in a non-production environment and monitor VPC Flow Logs to confirm that traffic traverses the expected path. Centralized inspection increases visibility and helps meet compliance requirements by applying uniform policies across your organization. Centralized inspection with a security VPC means use a security vpc plus transit gateway to centralize network firewall inspection and simplify policy consistency.. In practical terms, routing via transit gateway for consistent enforcement. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Centralized Inspection
Architecture

Security VPC + Transit Gateway

Centralize enforcement by routing traffic through a security VPC that hosts Network Firewall. This enables consistent rules for ingress, egress, and inter-VPC traffic.

Benefits: simplified policy updates, centralized logging, and easier compliance audits.
Pitfall: asymmetric routing breaks stateful inspection; ensure both directions traverse the firewall path.
Example Checklist
  • Configure Transit Gateway attachments for each VPC.
  • Route VPC egress through the security VPC subnets with firewall endpoints.
  • Validate return paths and NAT behavior for asymmetric traffic.
  • Enable Flow Logs for verification and auditing.
Key Takeaway

Centralization simplifies enforcement but requires careful routing so stateful inspection works correctly.

screens.title: VPC Flow Logs: what they record and why
screens.narratorSegment: VPC Flow Logs capture metadata about the IP traffic to and from network interfaces in your VPC. Each record includes source and destination IP addresses, source and destination ports, the protocol used, the number of bytes and packets transferred, timestamps, and an action indicator showing whether the traffic was accepted or rejected. Flow Logs can be published to CloudWatch Logs or S3, making them useful for real-time alerting or longer-term forensic analysis. For example, if an instance begins communicating with an unexpected external IP, flow logs reveal which internal interface initiated the connection, the destination port and protocol, the volume of data transferred, and whether security groups or NACLs allowed the flow. Integrating Flow Logs with a SIEM or Security Hub helps correlate network telemetry with other security signals. A common mistake is not retaining logs long enough for incident investigations; plan retention according to your compliance needs. Also, remember flow logs do not capture packet payloads—they provide flow metadata that supports rapid triage and pattern detection. VPC Flow Logs: what they record and why means flow logs give ip-level records of traffic flows for troubleshooting, detection, and auditing without capturing packet payloads.. In practical terms, telemetry for troubleshooting and security analysis. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. narration.text: VPC Flow Logs capture metadata about the IP traffic to and from network interfaces in your VPC. Flow Logs can be published to CloudWatch Logs or S3, making them useful for real-time alerting or longer-term forensic analysis. For example, if an instance begins communicating with an unexpected external IP, flow logs reveal which internal interface initiated the connection, the destination port and protocol, the volume of data transferred, and whether security groups or NACLs allowed the flow. Integrating Flow Logs with a SIEM or Security Hub helps correlate network telemetry with other security signals. A common mistake is not retaining logs long enough for incident investigations; plan retention according to your compliance needs. Also, remember flow logs do not capture packet payloads—they provide flow metadata that supports rapid triage and pattern detection. content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › CLI: Create Web ACL
Starter Commands
# 1. Create a Web ACL
aws wafv2 create-web-acl \
    --name MyWebAppACL \
    --scope REGIONAL \
    --default-action Allow={} \
    --visibility-config CloudWatchMetricsEnabled=true,MetricName=MyWebAppACL,SampledRequestsEnabled=true \
    --description "Web ACL for my web application"

# 2. Add an AWS Managed Rule Group (SQLi)
aws wafv2 update-web-acl \
    --name MyWebAppACL \
    --scope REGIONAL \
    --id  \
    --lock-token  \
    --default-action Allow={} \
    --visibility-config CloudWatchMetricsEnabled=true,MetricName=MyWebAppACL,SampledRequestsEnabled=true \
    --rules '[
        {
            "Name": "AWSManagedRulesSQLiRuleSet",
            "Priority": 1,
            "Statement": {
                "ManagedRuleGroupStatement": {
                    "VendorName": "AWS",
                    "Name": "AWSManagedRulesSQLiRuleSet"
                }
            },
            "Action": {"Block": {}},
            "VisibilityConfig": {"SampledRequestsEnabled": true,"CloudWatchMetricsEnabled": true,"MetricName": "AWSManagedRulesSQLiRuleSet"}
        }
    ]'

# 3. Associate the Web ACL with your ALB
aws wafv2 associate-web-acl \
    --web-acl-arn  \
    --resource-arn 

# 4. (Simulated) Test for SQLi
# curl "http:///?param=1%27%20OR%20%271%27%3D%271"  # Expect 403 if blocked
Replace placeholders with your values, run in a staging environment when possible, and check CloudWatch metrics and sampled requests to tune rules.
Practical Notes
  • Use REGIONAL scope for ALBs and GLOBAL for CloudFront.
  • Monitor sampled requests before changing actions to block.
  • Ensure IAM permissions for WAF operations and resource associations.

Run the create command, then run the update in count mode to gather telemetry before blocking traffic.

screens.title: Stateless vs Stateful rules in Network Firewall
screens.narratorSegment: Stateless and stateful rules serve different operational needs. Stateless rules inspect each packet independently and are efficient at high volumes for simple checks like IP or port blocking. They are deterministic and fast, making them suitable for initial packet filtering or blocking known bad IP ranges. Stateful rules track connection information and allow decisions based on session context, which is essential for protocols where the meaning of a packet depends on an established session. For example, allowing return packets for an established TCP connection requires stateful awareness. Stateful rules enable more advanced controls such as application protocol awareness or domain name inspection when combined with deeper packet inspection. A trade-off is that stateful inspection requires more resources and careful routing so both directions of the flow hit the firewall; asymmetric routing undermines stateful logic. Use stateless filters for broad, high-speed blocking and stateful rules when you need connection-aware decisions or IPS-style detection. Always test both rule types under realistic traffic so you understand performance and correctness impacts. Fast packet filtering. Each packet is evaluated independently, ideal for IP and port blocks and high-throughput needs.
Best practice
Use stateless rules for broad network filters and to reduce load on stateful inspection engines.

screens.narratorSegment: Operational hygiene is as important as technical controls. fullNarratorScript:
Network security is a continuous, layered effort. In this chapter we focus on a practical stack: a web application firewall for Layer 7 filtering, DDoS protections that handle volumetric and protocol attacks, a managed network firewall for centralized packet inspection, and VPC Flow Logs for visibility. You will learn what each service protects against, how they work together, and common mistakes to avoid. For example, WAF inspects HTTP requests to stop S Q L injection or cross-site scripting, while Shield handles large floods at the network and transport layers. Network Firewall enforces consistent rules at VPC boundaries, and Flow Logs give you the forensic data to investigate suspicious activity. We will also walk through a hands-on scenario: creating a Web ACL, adding an AWS managed SQLi rule group, and associating it with an ALB. By the end of this chapter you should be able to choose the right combination of controls, configure basic protections, and plan where to place centralized inspection. Consider: if your app is public and business-critical, which two controls are essential to start with, and why?

In this chapter you'll build practical competency across four areas of network protection. First, you will implement AWS WAF rules and rule groups to stop common web exploits; you should be able to pick a managed rule group and attach it to an Application Load Balancer. Second, you will understand how Shield Standard defends automatically and when Shield Advanced is appropriate; you'll learn the capabilities that justify paying for Advanced. Third, you will configure and manage AWS Network Firewall for centralized filtering, including an understanding of stateless versus stateful rules and how they affect traffic inspection. Fourth, you will deploy VPC Flow Logs and use them to monitor and investigate suspicious flows by reading source and destination IPs, ports, protocols, and accept or reject actions. Each objective pairs a practical skill with why it matters in reducing risk and improving incident response. By the end you will be able to propose a layered plan that uses these services together and avoid common configuration mistakes that can block legitimate traffic.

This second objectives slide expands the practical expectations: you'll be able to plan a centralized inspection architecture using Transit Gateway and a security VPC so that Network Firewall enforces consistent policies across many VPCs. You will also practice reading Flow Log records to identify source and destination IPs, ports, protocols, bytes transferred, and whether traffic was accepted or rejected. Lastly, you'll learn to avoid common mistakes: do not rely on a single control, do test WAF and firewall changes in non-production environments, and do put rollback procedures in place to avoid accidental disruption. These skills matter because security is not only about blocking attacks but also about maintaining availability and observability. A good exercise is to propose an enforcement point, pick a managed WAF rule group for S Q L injection, and list three telemetry fields you would monitor for suspicious behavior.

A layered security approach combines complementary controls to reduce risk, avoid single points of failure, and make incident response more effective. Start with security groups and network ACLs at the instance and subnet levels to provide basic filtering by port and IP. Add a perimeter layer that inspects HTTP traffic using an application firewall to stop exploits targeted at your code. Behind that, place a managed network firewall to perform deeper packet inspection and apply organization-wide policies. Finally, enable telemetry—VPC Flow Logs—to verify that policies are working and to investigate anomalies. A concrete example: an internet-facing web app can be fronted by an ALB with an attached WAF Web ACL blocking S Q L injection attempts. Shield Standard automatically mitigates most large floods at the network layer, and if the app is business-critical you would subscribe to Shield Advanced for DDoS response and cost protection. A common misconception is that more rules always improve security; in practice, overly aggressive rules can block legitimate traffic such as DNS and health checks. Testing changes in a staging environment and using count mode before blocking helps avoid outages. The key takeaway: design boundaries where they are most effective, collect telemetry to validate behavior, and plan rollback steps for any enforcement change.

AWS WAF is an application-layer filter that inspects HTTP and HTTPS requests to web applications and APIs. It looks at IP addresses, HTTP headers, the request body, and URI strings to match patterns associated with attacks such as S Q L injection or cross-site scripting. You can write custom rules for precise control, or attach managed rule groups curated by AWS or third parties for common protections. Managed rule groups are useful when you want fast coverage for known vulnerability classes without authoring detailed patterns yourself. When a request matches a rule, WAF can take one of three actions: allow, block, or count for monitoring. A practical example: attach a managed SQLi rule group to a Web ACL protecting an ALB that fronts an A P I. The WAF will examine incoming requests and block those matching the S Q L injection patterns, returning a 403 response. A misunderstanding to avoid is thinking WAF replaces code-level validation; WAF reduces attack surface but input validation and secure coding remain necessary. Always enable visibility configuration to send sampled requests and metrics to CloudWatch so you can tune rules based on real traffic.

WAF offers a flexible rule model. You can create rules that match on IP addresses, HTTP headers, URI strings, and request bodies. Rules may look for signature patterns that indicate S Q L injection or cross-site scripting. Managed rule groups give you an easy starting point — for example, a S Q L database managed rule group targets S Q L injection patterns so you do not have to author every detection pattern yourself. Start with managed protections in count mode to see what traffic would have been blocked and tune the rule priorities before switching to block. Use IP sets to block or allow ranges quickly. For custom rules, think about rule order and priorities because WAF evaluates rules based on priority. A concrete tuning example: deploy the managed SQLi rule group and monitor CloudWatch metrics for the Web ACL; if you see many false positives from a legitimate bot, add a conditional rule to allow that bot's user agent or IP range. A frequent error is setting a broad block action that inadvertently denies legitimate health checks or partners. Always validate rules with sampled request logs and plan a rollback path in case a change disrupts availability.

AWS Shield provides DDoS protection at different levels. Shield Standard is automatic and free for all customers. It provides always-on detection and inline mitigation for common Layer 3 and Layer 4 attacks, such as SYN floods, UDP floods, and amplification attacks, and it works transparently with CloudFront, Route 53, and load balancers. Shield Advanced is a paid tier intended for business-critical applications. It offers near real-time attack visibility, engages the AWS DDoS Response Team for proactive mitigation, and includes cost protection to cover scaling charges that occur during an attack. Shield Advanced also integrates with WAF so that the response team can suggest or deploy custom WAF rules during an attack. A common confusion is to assume Shield Advanced prevents every possible outage; it significantly improves detection and response but must be combined with WAF and network controls as part of a layered design. For most standard workloads, Shield Standard is sufficient; for high-value services with strict availability requirements, Shield Advanced provides operational support and financial protections that justify its use. AWS Shield: Standard vs Advanced means shield standard is automatic; shield advanced adds visibility, drt support, and cost protections for critical workloads.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

AWS Network Firewall is a managed network and transport layer service that filters traffic moving through VPC boundaries. It supports both stateless rules, which examine packets independently for fast filtering, and stateful rules, which track connections and enable deeper inspection of protocols and application behavior. Stateful rules are useful when you need to make decisions based on connection state or application-layer knowledge, such as allowing established TLS flows or inspecting HTTP headers. Network Firewall can be deployed in a centralized security VPC so that traffic from many VPCs is routed through a single enforcement point via Transit Gateway. This centralization simplifies policy consistency and compliance. A practical scenario: route all egress traffic from development VPCs through the security VPC where Network Firewall enforces outbound domain and port rules, preventing data exfiltration to risky hosts. A common misunderstanding is treating Network Firewall as a replacement for WAF; instead, they complement each other: WAF handles Layer 7 web application threats, while Network Firewall enforces network-level policies and can perform intrusion prevention tasks. AWS Network Firewall overview means network firewall provides stateless and stateful filtering and fits well in a centralized security vpc for consistent policy enforcement.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Centralized inspection uses a security VPC that hosts Network Firewall and other monitoring appliances. Traffic from application or data VPCs is routed through a Transit Gateway to the security VPC, creating a single enforcement point for ingress, egress, and inter-VPC flows. This architecture simplifies policy management because you maintain rules in one place instead of spread across multiple VPCs. A concrete scenario: route egress traffic from several development VPCs to the security VPC where Network Firewall enforces outbound deny lists and inspects HTTPS connections for suspicious domains. Ensure routing and NAT are configured so that return traffic flows back through the inspection path. A common pitfall is creating asymmetric routing where return packets bypass the firewall, which prevents stateful rules from working correctly. Test the routing in a non-production environment and monitor VPC Flow Logs to confirm that traffic traverses the expected path. Centralized inspection increases visibility and helps meet compliance requirements by applying uniform policies across your organization. Each record includes source and destination IP addresses, source and destination ports, the protocol used, the number of bytes and packets transferred, timestamps, and an action indicator showing whether the traffic was accepted or rejected. Stateless and stateful rules serve different operational needs. Stateless rules inspect each packet independently and are efficient at high volumes for simple checks like IP or port blocking. They are deterministic and fast, making them suitable for initial packet filtering or blocking known bad IP ranges. Stateful rules track connection information and allow decisions based on session context, which is essential for protocols where the meaning of a packet depends on an established session. For example, allowing return packets for an established TCP connection requires stateful awareness. Stateful rules enable more advanced controls such as application protocol awareness or domain name inspection when combined with deeper packet inspection. A trade-off is that stateful inspection requires more resources and careful routing so both directions of the flow hit the firewall; asymmetric routing undermines stateful logic. Use stateless filters for broad, high-speed blocking and stateful rules when you need connection-aware decisions or IPS-style detection. Always test both rule types under realistic traffic so you understand performance and correctness impacts.
